paragraphs.heading: The Sun as a climate driver
paragraphs.text: Across geologic time, which spans millions to billions of years, the patterns of solar irradiance and of solar variation have been one of the main drivers of climate change. The evidence comes from many timescales and many sources. These include direct observations, composites built from different proxy observations, and numerical climate models.

paragraphs.heading: The faint young Sun
paragraphs.text: Three to four billion years ago the Sun gave off only 70% of its current power. With the atmosphere Earth has today, that would not have been enough to keep water from freezing everywhere. Yet evidence points to liquid water existing already in the Hadean and Archean eons. This puzzle is known as the faint young Sun paradox. One proposed answer is a vastly different atmosphere, holding much higher concentrations of greenhouse gases than exist now.

paragraphs.heading: Billions of years, both directions
paragraphs.text: Over the roughly 4 billion years that followed, the Sun's energy output increased and the makeup of Earth's atmosphere changed. Over the next five billion years the Sun will die, turning first into a red giant that is very bright and then into a white dwarf that is very faint. That will have dramatic effects on climate, and the red giant phase is likely to end any life on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the Sun
paragraphs.text: Since 1978 satellites have measured solar irradiance directly, with very good accuracy. These measurements show total solar irradiance going up and down by 0.1% across the roughly 11 years of the solar cycle, while its average value has been stable since the measurements began. Before the 1970s, solar irradiance is estimated from proxy variables such as tree rings, sunspot counts and the abundance of cosmogenic isotopes like ¹⁰Be, all calibrated to the direct measurements made after 1978. Since the 1960s solar activity has been trending downward. In solar cycles 19 to 24 the maximum number of sunspots was 201, 111, 165, 159, 121 and 82.

paragraphs.heading: The Little Ice Age question
paragraphs.text: One long-term historical correlation between solar activity and climate is the Maunder minimum of 1645–1715. It was a period of little or no sunspot activity, and it partly overlapped the Little Ice Age, when cold weather prevailed in Europe. The Little Ice Age covered roughly the 16th to the 19th centuries. It is debated whether the cooling was caused by the low solar activity or by other factors. A 2012 paper linked the Little Ice Age instead to volcanism, pointing to an unusual 50-year episode in which four large, sulfur-rich explosive eruptions took place. The paper claimed that explaining the cold does not require large changes in solar irradiance.

paragraphs.heading: Not the cause of recent warming
paragraphs.text: In recent decades spacecraft have observed both solar activity and Earth's climate with unprecedented accuracy, and these observations show unequivocally that changes in the Sun are not the cause of recent global warming. The Sun in the modern era has stayed within a band narrow enough that climate has been little affected. Climate models that consider only variations in total solar irradiance and volcanic activity have been unable to reproduce the rapid warming seen in recent decades. Human-induced forcings are needed to reproduce the warming of the late 20th century. A 2010 paper suggested that a new period of low solar activity lasting 90 years would lower global average temperatures by about 0.3 °C, far too little to offset the increased forcing from greenhouse gases.

paragraphs.heading: Why the direct effect is small
paragraphs.text: Changes in solar irradiance affect the climate directly, but this is generally considered a minor effect. The measured variations are too small to have a significant effect unless some process amplifies them. The ultraviolet part of sunlight varies by more than the total. So if ultraviolet had a disproportionate effect, for a reason not yet known, that might explain a larger solar signal.
